children.value: Your crates can depend on other libraries from

repositories, or subdirectories on your local file system. You can also temporarily override the location of a dependency — for example, to be able to test out a bug fix in the dependency that you are working on locally. You can have different dependencies for different platforms, and dependencies that are only used during development. Let’s take a look at how to do each of these.

It is possible to specify both a registry version and a
dependency will be used locally (in which case the
is checked against the local copy), and when published to a registry like
, it will use the registry version. Other combinations are not allowed. Examples:

children.code:
[dependencies]
# Uses `my-bitflags` when used locally, and uses
# version 1.0 from crates.io when published.
bitflags = { path = "my-bitflags", version = "1.0" }

# Uses the given git repo when used locally, and uses
# version 1.0 from crates.io when published.
smallvec = { git = "https://github.com/servo/rust-smallvec.git", version = "1.0" }

# Note: if a version doesn't match, Cargo will fail to compile!

If a package you depend on offers conditional features, you can specify which to use:

children.code:
[dependencies.awesome]
version = "1.3.5"
default-features = false # do not include the default features, and optionally
                         # cherry-pick individual features
features = ["secure-password", "civet"]

the key you write for a dependency typically matches up to the name of the crate you import from in the code. For some projects, though, you may wish to reference the crate with a different name in the code regardless of how it’s published on crates.io. For example you may wish to:
Depend on multiple versions of a crate.
Depend on crates with the same name from different registries.
To support this Cargo supports a
section of which package should be depended on:

children.code:
[package]
name = "mypackage"
version = "0.0.1"

[dependencies]
foo = "0.1"
bar = { git = "https://github.com/example/project.git", package = "foo" }
baz = { version = "0.1", registry = "custom", package = "foo" }

children.value: In this example, three crates are now available in your Rust code:

children.code:
extern crate foo; // crates.io
extern crate bar; // git repository
extern crate baz; // registry `custom`
